# An all-point layer-cake identity for the mixed-depth envelope

This note integrates the actual-source envelope over the original mixed measure, including points and entire fibers which no affine-cost selector exposes. It proves an exact global deficit identity and an explicit geometric lower budget. It does not supply an OC mass bound or an unproved slab-coverage assertion.

## 1. Definitions and the canonical selected slope

Let C be a convex body in R^n times R^d, d>=1, with positive mixed d-volume. Let S be its intersection with the mixed lattice, let mu be the sum of d-volume over the finitely many integer fibers, and let M=mu(S)>0. At Y in S, let D(Y) be raw mixed halfspace depth, f(Y) raw ordinary own-fiber depth, and F(Y)=f(Y)^(1/d). Put f=F=0 on zero-volume fibers. All of these are defined using the original closed ambient halfspaces and the original mixed measure.

Use the scalar envelope established in
`candidate 8280d34e5808dfad`:

    E(lambda)=max_S [D(Y)+lambda F(Y)], lambda>=0,
    Q=max_S D,
    a=max{F(Y):D(Y)=Q},
    b=max_S F,
    Dtop=max{D(Y):F(Y)=b}.

At each lambda choose the largest active F value, denoted g(lambda). Its associated actual depth is D_lambda=E(lambda)-lambda g(lambda). The proved envelope properties are

    g(0)=a,  g is nondecreasing and right-continuous,
    lim_(lambda->infinity) g(lambda)=b,
    E'_+(lambda)=g(lambda),
    integral_(0,infinity) lambda dg(lambda)=Q-Dtop.       (1)

The source points themselves need not be chosen as a measurable path. Only the canonical scalar g is used below.

For a<s<b define the generalized inverse

    Lambda(s)=inf{lambda>=0:g(lambda)>=s}.                (2)

It is finite and nondecreasing on this open interval. Its values at a and b can be assigned arbitrarily for Lebesgue integration, including infinity at b. If a=b, every integral over (a,b) below is zero.

Define the convex nondecreasing deficit function on [0,b] by

    C(t)=0,                         0<=t<=a,
    C(t)=integral_a^t Lambda(s) ds, a<t<=b.              (3)

## 2. Exact conjugate and endpoint formulas

For every t in [0,b],

    C(t)=sup_(lambda>=0) [Q+lambda t-E(lambda)]
        =integral_0^infinity (t-g(lambda))_+ d lambda.   (4)

In particular,

    C(b)=Q-Dtop.                                      (5)

Proof. The convex Lipschitz envelope is absolutely continuous on every bounded interval and has right derivative g. Hence

    E(lambda)-Q=integral_0^lambda g(r) dr.

For fixed t, the integrand t-g(r) is nonincreasing. Its positive part occupies an initial interval, possibly empty or unbounded. The supremum of its initial integrals is therefore the integral of its positive part. This proves the first equality in (4), including intervals where g=t.

Tonelli gives

    integral_0^infinity (t-g(r))_+ dr
      =integral_a^t |{r>=0:g(r)<s}| ds.

For a<s<b, the set in the inner measure is an initial interval of length Lambda(s). A possible endpoint changes no length. A jump of g therefore contributes an interval of s values with the same inverse value; no jump mass is lost. This proves (3)–(4).

For t=b, Tonelli and the right-continuous Stieltjes measure give

    integral_0^infinity [b-g(r)] dr
      =integral_0^infinity integral_(r,infinity) dg(lambda) dr
      =integral_(0,infinity) lambda dg(lambda).

There is no contribution from an atom at zero, and g(0)=a already fixes the starting slope. Equation (1) proves (5), so all displayed integrals are finite. In particular C is finite and continuous also at b. QED.

## 3. Every original point pays its own deficit

For EVERY Y in S, whether or not selected by any scalar or vector cost,

    C(F(Y)) <= Q-D(Y).                                (6)

Indeed D(Y)+lambda F(Y)<=E(lambda) for each lambda; rearrange and take the supremum in (4). Define the nonnegative remainder

    J(Y)=Q-D(Y)-C(F(Y)).                               (7)

Then the exact all-point identity is

    M Q-integral_S D dmu
      = integral_a^b Lambda(s) mu{Y:F(Y)>s} ds
                       +integral_S J dmu.             (8)

Proof. F and D are continuous on each positive fiber and zero on zero-volume fibers, so J is measurable. All terms are finite: 0<=C(F)<=Q and 0<=J<=Q. Equation (3), Tonelli, and the defining equality (7) give (8). Strict versus weak F level sets does not affect this integral: for each fixed Y, the singleton endpoint s=F(Y) has zero Lebesgue measure. This argument does not assume individual level boundaries are null. QED.

Equivalently the same identity has a direct parameter-layer form:

    integral_S C(F) dmu
      =integral_0^infinity integral_S (F(Y)-g(lambda))_+ dmu d lambda.

This counts original points with multiplicity determined explicitly by their own-depth roots. It does not assert that selected-source slabs cover those points.

If Y maximizes D+lambda F at any finite lambda, then J(Y)=0: that lambda makes the supremum in (4) equal Q-D(Y). At t=b, the points of the top own-depth level with D=Dtop also have J=0, whether or not a finite parameter exposes them. The remainder J thus retains the genuinely unpaid deficit of hidden points; it may not be discarded in an equality or inferred to vanish everywhere.

## 4. A proved geometric lower bound for the all-point charge

Let V_z be the positive fiber volumes and Gamma=(d/(d+1))^d. For every s>=0,

    mu{F>s} >= sum_z V_z
                  [1-s/(Gamma V_z)^(1/d)]_+^d.         (9)

To prove this, choose the ordinary centroid c_z of each positive fiber. Ordinary Grünbaum gives F(z,c_z)>=(Gamma V_z)^(1/d). Concavity of F and its nonnegativity on the whole fiber imply that the homothetic body

    c_z + [1-s/(Gamma V_z)^(1/d)] (C_z-c_z)

lies in {F>=s} when the coefficient is nonnegative. Applying the same inclusion at s+epsilon gives a subset of {F>s}; let epsilon decrease to zero. This proves the volume bound without a level-boundary regularity assumption. The sum is finite.

Consequently (8) yields the genuine original-volume budget

    M Q >= integral_S D dmu
      + integral_a^b Lambda(s) sum_z V_z
             [1-s/(Gamma V_z)^(1/d)]_+^d ds.           (10)

One may further use D>=f and integrate (9), with t=f and s=t^(1/d), to obtain

    integral_S D dmu >= integral_S f dmu
             >= [Gamma/binom(2d,d)] sum_z V_z^2.       (11)

The elementary integral is

    integral_0^1 [1-t^(1/d)]^d dt
      = d integral_0^1 r^(d-1)(1-r)^d dr
      = 1/binom(2d,d).

Thus (10) and (11) give an explicit necessary scalar budget for the original geometry. The own-depth level-volume comparison and its first-moment bound were already established in `candidate 9402605e47a1b4ef`; the new point here is their integration against the actual mixed-depth envelope's inverse slope, with every endpoint and hidden-point remainder retained.

## 5. A sharp reason this charge is not automatic mass coverage

Take n=1, any d>=1, an odd integer N>=3, and a centrally symmetric d-dimensional convex body B with center zero and volume V. Let

    C=[0,N-1] times B,
    S={0,...,N-1} times B.

Then M=NV and all fibers are strictly nonheavy at the n=1 threshold: V<M/2. At the actual point Y=((N-1)/2,0), central symmetry of S shows that every nonvertical through-point closed halfspace has mass exactly M/2. A vertical through-point halfspace contains at least (N+1)V/2. Thus D(Y)=M/2. At any point, two opposing nonvertical through-point halfspaces have null common boundary and masses summing to M, so Q=M/2.

Each own fiber has maximal ordinary depth V/2 at zero. Therefore this SAME mixed deepest point has F=b=(V/2)^(1/d). Hence

    a=b,  Dtop=Q,  E(lambda)=Q+lambda b,
    g(lambda)=b,  C identically zero.

The new all-point envelope charge is zero on every original fiber, although the total original mass is NV and can be made arbitrarily large relative to one fiber. Formula (8) remains exactly correct: its entire deficit is the remainder integral. Thus neither a positive fraction of original mass nor a positive number of selected-source slabs is forced by the envelope work alone, even in a strict-noheavy body with regular positive fibers.

This example lies above the OC target and is not a counterexample to OC or to a mechanism restricted to hypothetical below-target bodies. It demonstrates the precise gap: (8) supplies a global accounting law, but a further geometric relation involving the remainder or the below-target regime is required to extract the factor 2^n. No such relation is proved here. Treating that missing relation as a coverage lemma would simply reopen the unproved global step.
